en: Preface to the *Commentary on the Practice of Samatha and Vipaśyanā: Transmitted Decisions for the Propagation*.
If one adheres to the doctrine of emptiness and non-existence, the Way of Name and Teaching will fall into ruin. If one discards written words, the purpose of composition will be subverted.
Long ago, the Brahma King, seizing the opportune moment, appeared for the benefit of the world; his sagehood and worthiness were in accord with the Way, and his virtuous reputation was heard afar.
Do not violate this.
We must still rely on verbal expression to entrust [the teachings] to those who collect them;
how much more so now that time has long passed into the Semblance Age, when learning is meager and few possess the discernment of the subtle.
Among those guests who grasp this meaning, not even one or two in ten exist.
There are even those who sit in silence for years, content with their dull ignorance;
they reach old age debating the mind, lingering in hesitation over the doctrines of "half" and "full."
How could the manifold deviations of people be otherwise?
Before even ascending the steps, they grasp at the elephant's form, each describing its color and features.
Some say that "the mind itself is Buddha" is the gateway to awakening and entry.
Form is not different from emptiness; from beginning to end, who leaves a trace?
As all things merge into the cessation of dependence, what use are chapters and verses?
Alas! The great teaching has declined to such an extent.
For it is because the nature of syllables has not yet been discerned that nothing can illustrate the profound efficacy of the *dhāraṇī*.
Long ago, when the Great Master Zhizhe descended to manifest himself in this world,
he extensively propagated his profound virtue and greatly rescued the world from its turbulent currents.
He consulted the great thoughts of Nāgārjuna to restore the severed threads of the Dharma,
and he commanded his house to follow ancient precedents by taking Madhyamaka as its master lineage.
He established the ultimate standard and articulated his teachings, taking the Mahāyāna as his final refuge.
Thereupon, the empowerment was conferred.
Master Ding drew out and extended its principles;
reverently upholding them, he composed extensive records and commentaries.
The gates and windows of the teachings have been brightly illuminated once again from this point forward.
This was followed by Master Weihua;
Master Wei had cultivated roots of merit in past lives, never deviating from his original vow.
Furthermore, Tian-gong Wei respectfully received [the teaching] from Gong-jing like water being passed from one vessel to another,
and transmitted it to Zuo-xi Xuan-lang.
Master Lang was preeminent, possessing a singular and decisive celestial intuition.
While others followed conventional interpretations of the teachings, he had no leisure to worry about my prose;
he resoundingly propagated them at the Vimalakīrti altar, remaining profoundly serene.
However, while still a youth with hair tied in two tufts, Gongsian was exceptionally brilliant and insightful;
Zuo Xi deeply recognized his extraordinary potential and vowed to transmit the Lamp to him.
He once remarked that the two gates of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) encompass all spiritual practices.
The establishment of the Perfect and Sudden [teaching] unifies all through a single principle. Alas!
Having succeeded four generations, its duration has nearly reached two hundred years.
The errors between "yu" and "lu" are not without their similarities and differences;
I am now about to unravel these thoughts to guide others toward the profound current,
thereby extensively refuting heterodox doubts that have proliferated throughout antiquity and the present.
Substantial yet not vulgar, extensive yet not prolix,
he authored the *Fuxingji* (Record of Auxiliary Explanations) in ten fascicles.
It fully embodies the principles of the broad and concise teachings of former sages and accords with the capacities for excellence or inferiority of people today.
How could it be merely a matter of interweaving what one has heard? It is intended to encompass and synthesize what one governs.
What is governed is the immediate ascent through the wondrous operation of the "Three Multiples" (san-duo);
what is heard is the profound insight into the mystery of the "One Reality" (yi-zhen). These two are essentially identical.
Now, when the path of practice has its divergent routes, the beginning and the end are separated by heaven;
yet when liberation is without fixed boundaries, there are still degrees of depth according to one's capacity.
Therefore, I shall establish these expositions to support practice, so as to present the whole in its completeness.
Therefore, people have come from afar to inquire about their doubts and request further instruction.
Day and night they have diligently struck away ignorance and uncovered what was hidden,
hoping to provide profound assistance, act with reverent accordance to the Way, and transmit its broad propagation.
When the Way is about to be propagated, its movement is not solitary.
I, a student of the final age, venture to offer light reflections upon the Supreme Vehicle;
this is like a torch adding luster to the two luminaries.
Preface respectfully composed by Jinshan Chujin, son of Pumen,
during the first day of the year of Yongtai, the fourth year of the eighth generation of the Tang dynasty.
